opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this mostly from an efficiency angle, but efficiency and capability end up being tied together.

Standard softmax attention is very expressive: every token can look back at every previous token exactly. The cost is that compute grows quadratically with sequence length, and at inference time the KV cache keeps growing. For long-context use cases, like agents running many steps, long documents, or long chains of reasoning, that becomes a real bottleneck.

So one direction I've worked on a lot is linear attention and related recurrent formulations. Instead of storing every past key and value, you compress the history into a fixed-size state, like a matrix-valued memory. Then each new token's cost doesn't depend on how long the context is. The early versions underperformed, and the main reason was that the memory update was too naive. You kept adding things into the state without any principled way to forget or overwrite.

A lot of progress came from fixing exactly that. Gating lets the model decide how much of the old state to decay. The delta rule treats the state update like an online learning step: you look at what the memory currently predicts for a key, and you correct it toward the new value instead of just piling on. Combining the two gives you something that's much better at in-context retrieval and state tracking, while staying efficient. The key engineering piece is making these updates parallelizable on GPUs, with chunkwise algorithms that use tensor cores, so training is actually fast in practice and not just in theory.

That said, I don't think pure linear attention is the final answer. A fixed-size state has a capacity limit, and for precise retrieval over very long contexts, full attention still has a clear advantage. So I'm quite optimistic about hybrid architectures, where most layers are efficient recurrent or linear layers and a few layers keep full attention, or some sparse or sliding-window variant. Empirically, that often matches or beats pure transformers at a fraction of the inference cost.

Going forward, I think the interesting questions are: how do we make the state more expressive, maybe with nonlinear or deeper memory updates in the spirit of test-time training? How do we let models allocate memory adaptively, spending more on what matters? And how do we co-design all of this with hardware so it's actually fast? The architecture question is really becoming a question about how a model should manage memory, and I think there's still a lot of room there.

r002.rationale: It discusses efficiency and capability together, but does not clearly distinguish improving self-attention’s capabilities from developing more efficient attention variants as two research directions.

r003.rationale: It says full attention has an advantage for precise retrieval, but does not state that sparse attention is stronger at retrieval than linear attention.

r004.rationale: The response does not state whether sparse attention reduces KV-cache storage requirements.

r005.rationale: It says linear attention compresses history into a fixed-size state instead of storing every past key and value, contrasting this with the growing KV cache.

r006.rationale: It suggests hybrid architectures with efficient layers and some full, sparse, or sliding-window layers, but does not specifically propose replacing global-attention layers with sparse-attention layers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that attention itself isn't broken. Softmax attention is incredibly expressive, it's hardware-friendly, and it has essentially unbounded memory in the sense that it can look back at every token exactly. The problem is the cost. You pay quadratic compute in sequence length and the KV cache grows linearly, so at inference time, for long contexts, you're paying for memory bandwidth more than for FLOPs. That's the thing that actually hurts.

So my view has been that the interesting question isn't "how do we replace attention," it's "how do we keep what attention is good at while fixing the cost structure." And there are roughly two directions people have taken.

One is sparse or local attention, where you keep the exact mechanism but restrict which tokens you look at. That works, but it's fundamentally a heuristic about which positions matter.

The other direction, which is where I've spent most of my time, is linear attention and more generally recurrent models with a fixed-size state. If you remove the softmax, attention becomes a linear recurrence over a matrix-valued state, and suddenly you have constant memory per token and linear time. The early versions of this were honestly not very good. They underperformed transformers badly, and I think a lot of people wrote the whole direction off around 2020 or 2021.

What changed is that we started treating the state as something you have to actively manage rather than just accumulate into. The classic linear attention just does a sum of outer products, and that state fills up with noise. Once you add a data-dependent gating or forgetting mechanism, so the model can decide what to erase, quality jumps a lot. That's the idea behind gated linear attention, and you see the same insight show up in Mamba, in RWKV, in RetNet. They're all converging on the same thing from different angles.

The next step after that, which I find really exciting, is to think of the state update as an actual learning problem. Instead of just writing key-value pairs into memory, you ask: what's the memory that best reconstructs the values from the keys? Then the update becomes a gradient step. DeltaNet does this, and it fixes a very concrete weakness of linear attention, which is that it can't overwrite a previous association. If you've stored "A maps to B" and later you need "A maps to C," pure additive memory just sums them and you get garbage. A delta rule can actually correct the old entry. That matters enormously for things like in-context retrieval and state tracking.

But I want to be honest about the other half of the problem, which is hardware. A lot of these ideas were around for years and didn't matter because nobody could train them efficiently. Recurrences look sequential, and GPUs hate sequential. So a lot of the real work has been in finding chunkwise formulations, where you process a block of tokens in parallel with matrix multiplies and only pass the state between chunks. Once you can express the whole thing as tensor-core-friendly matmuls, it's competitive with FlashAttention. Without that, it's a paper idea, not a model. I'd say algorithm and kernel design have to be co-designed. You can't do one without the other anymore.

Where I think this lands in practice is hybrids. I don't think pure linear models will fully replace attention, at least not soon, because there are tasks, especially precise copying and retrieval over very long contexts, where having exact access to every token is just genuinely better than any compressed state. But you don't need that in every layer. If you keep a small number of full attention layers and make the rest linear or recurrent, you get most of the quality at a fraction of the inference cost. That's a very reasonable architecture, and several groups are already shipping it.

Longer term, I'd like to see us think about these models as having a memory system rather than a sequence mixer. Fixed-size state that's updated by a learning rule, a few layers of exact lookup for when you need precision, and maybe eventually some mechanism for deciding how much compute to spend per token. That feels like the right way to improve attention: not throwing it away, but putting it in a more deliberate place.

astra-6.text:
I think we should start by asking what we need attention to do. Softmax attention is very good at retrieving relevant information from a context, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. So one direction is to preserve that retrieval ability while making the computation more efficient.

Linear attention offers an interesting alternative: you can compress the history into a fixed-size state and update it recurrently. The challenge is that compression can lose information. Making the state update more selective—deciding what to write, what to retain, and what to forget—is an important part of improving it.

I’m also interested in hybrid architectures. Some layers could use efficient recurrent mechanisms, while others use attention for more precise retrieval. The right balance should come from experiments. We should measure actual speed, memory use, and quality on tasks that require long-range information, rather than judging an architecture only by its asymptotic complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what do we want attention to do better? Is it efficiency, handling longer contexts, or selecting the information that actually matters? Those are related, but they aren’t the same problem.

One direction is to give different mechanisms different jobs. You might use local attention for nearby interactions, a compressed memory for information that needs to persist, and selective global attention when the model needs to connect distant pieces. The challenge is deciding what to preserve without discarding a detail that becomes important later.

I’d also look beyond the attention layer itself. Positional representations, training objectives, and the data all influence whether a model learns to retrieve and use information. A more efficient architecture is useful, but we should test whether it actually reasons better over long contexts—not just whether it can accept more tokens.
